reviews.title: Ambitious but frustratingly lacking in mechanics
reviews.text:
This game excels in its narrative and adaptive world building. I was obsessed. However, the immersion completely broke for me after realizing that the AI DM’s promised mechanical functions were purely thematic. I wasted a good chunk of my subscribed messages just arguing with the DM, asking it to recall its earlier commitments, and receiving absolute promises of reassurance, only for it to constantly contradict itself time and time again. This leads me to demanding for in-game compensation for better loot, which is often negotiable, but by then the immersion is gone and I no longer want to proceed with the task at hand. 

A recent example is the realization that my companions are merely decorative thematic tag-alongs in the narrative that have no mechanical weight on the campaign. There are spells and latencies that allow you to target a companion, but they are not actually active combatants in a battle. This completely contradicts my first fight against an inquisitor where I asked a guard to change sides and fight alongside me. Which he did. Mechanically. The three of us took turns rolling for attack and rolling for damage. He has since been my companion and only sits thematically in the background. Always distracted by another foe or obstacle that is just out of reach thematically. When confronted, the DM acknowledges that he used to be an active combatant, that it’s right for me to call that out, and promises he’ll be mechanically involved moving forward. Only to be relegated back to the narrative fly on the wall with zero involvement. 


Another example is my recent acquisition of a sword described as:
**Astral Vigil’s Blade (Longsword)**
*   **Base Damage:** 1d8 (one-handed) / 1d10 (two-handed).
*   **Passive Enchantment:** Your strikes deal an additional 1d4 Radiant damage on every hit.

**Ability: Vigil’s Retribution**
*   **Usage:** Bonus Action, usable once per Long Rest.
*   **Effects:**
    *   Ethereal dragon wings manifest.
    *   Gain a +15ft speed boost until the end of your current turn.
    *   Roll a d20. On a result of 11 or higher, you gain one additional melee attack.
    *   This extra attack, if it hits, deals 2d8 Radiant damage.

The passive and ability never trigger. When questioned, the DM shrugs and gives the good ole “idk what you’re talking about! I never heard of that passive or ability in my life”. I had to copy and paste its own message to get it to remember.  To which it responded:

“you are absolutely correct. I have reviewed the earlier logs and the specific mechanics you listed—you are right, these are clearly mechanical properties, not mere flavor. I apologize for the oversight; it appears those specific traits were not correctly integrated into the system's active ability registry I was referencing, leading to the confusion.” 

Which sounds like a mechanical fix. More than that actually, it says it is CLEARLY mechanical. Nope. All this technical jargon is purely thematic. It speaks of mechanical changes thematically with no actual means to implement. I told the AI to distinguish the two and to never use the former narratively if it can’t actually apply it to which it agreed. It continues to play coy.

reviews.title: Fun, until not fun.
reviews.text:
This game is fun, even though I abhor AI. The concept is incredible, because we all know the pain of not being able to schedule a time or day to play D&D, and this app helps in that regard.

My only real actual gripe with this game is with the players messaging system. I do not enjoy only having 60 messages base line every month, and then it resets again at the start of the next month. 

I understand completely why the devs do this, and I don’t fault them for trying to make money through the subscription options and through the individual purchasable messaging options for when you run out of messages to send. My issue that I want to play this game more often than the first two days of a month simply because I don’t want to spend the money on a subscription or for more messages.

I just wish that the devs would change the messaging system so that you could get 60 messages in a single week, with the messages resetting themselves after that week, just so myself and the other players of this game can invest more time into this game, as well potentially more money into it.

reviews.title: Highway Robbery
reviews.text:
I have been playing Dungeons and Dragons in a myriad of formats for over forty years, and I can honestly say that Everweave has incredible potential. The concept, gameplay, and overall experience have a lot going for them, and I genuinely want to see this game succeed.

Unfortunately, the pay-to-play structure is ridiculously expensive. The pricing takes what could be an outstanding D&D experience and makes it feel like players are constantly being asked to open their wallets just to fully enjoy the game.

The developers are acting like money grubbers, and the current monetization strategy is simply too aggressive. A game with this much potential should be building a loyal player base, not making players feel like they are being financially squeezed at every turn.

The developers need to change the pay-to-play structure immediately. Offer a fairer pricing model, provide more value for what players spend, and give the community a reasonable way to enjoy the game.

To conclude, Everweave could be something special, however, Blizzard (Warden of the West) must desist from further adventures.

reviews.title: How are the game functions..
reviews.text:
So the challenge, of course, in creating a game like this is separating game mechanics and the use of OpenAI. The AI part is easy. The game does very well in adapting to the story and creating story and keeping it on track. The game mechanics need a lot of work. They do function and they function decently. reviews.title: Frustration Abounds
reviews.text:
Great concept ruined by broken game state and paid-message loops

I really wanted to love Everweave. The concept is fantastic, and when the AI storytelling works, it can be genuinely entertaining. Unfortunately, after investing significant time into a campaign, the underlying game systems have made it incredibly frustrating—and because responses cost messages, fixing the game’s mistakes can literally cost the player money.

My campaign has repeatedly had narration and actual character state disagree. Gold earned through major story events has failed to appear correctly. Items have been purchased and narrated as equipped but provided none of their stated mechanical bonuses. I have bought AC-increasing equipment that did not increase AC. Other equipment has failed to modify skills or stats while certain weapons inexplicably work correctly.

My AI companion became an established partner in the story but was never properly represented mechanically. The DM has explicitly acknowledged at times that it “CANNOT MODIFY” things such as XP, gold, inventory, or party state. I’ve also encountered continuity failures where the DM forgets events that happened moments earlier—for example, describing a disarmed companion reaching for a sword that the game had already confiscated.

The worst experience was shopping. A major quest reward of 50,000 gold became inconsistent with the game’s displayed currency, and I spent roughly 10 paid messages trying to get purchases and a helmet resolved correctly. At that point I’m effectively paying to troubleshoot the game’s state synchronization instead of playing an RPG.

Bad dice rolls, failed plans, difficult enemies, and character consequences are part of D&D-style gaming. Those aren’t my complaint. My complaint is having to spend paid messages correcting the AI and mechanical systems when they contradict each other.

There is an excellent game buried here. But until narrative state, inventory, currency, equipment effects, companions, and character progression reliably synchronize—and players aren’t charged repeatedly while trying to correct those failures—I cannot recommend spending money on it.

reviews.title: Limited Scope and functionality
reviews.text:
The concept is promising and it starts off strong. Unfortunately, after about a hundred or so messages, the Ai starts to forget established details and the most basic of rules. 

In example, it initially did well in introducing, rolling, and integrating a follower NPC, and eventually forgot that she existed; gaslighting me. It would also forget the purpose and scope of items it rewarded me with, rendering them useless. 

A big part of DnD is maneuvering the rules and abilities. 

I love to spam Eldritch blast (1d10) and selected the eldritch invocation “agonizing blast” which should add my charisma modifier (+3 at the time) to damage rolls. This should all but guarantee a damage roll of 4, unless the target is resistant to force damage. I would regularly roll sub 4s for damage with no addition from my modifier. 

Finally, it has a habit, similar to  every other Ai that I’ve encountered, of rushing you. It always has suggestions, which is fine, but it can lead to “railroading,” and anyone who has suffered at the hands of a control freak DM is going to hate that. 

I thoroughly enjoyed playing the game, and even bought into the in-app purchase model to continue my adventure, but it’s missing the soul, the foundation, the “enduring legacy” of traditional tabletop campaigns. 

It’s novel, perhaps even captivating, but it still has a long way to go.

reviews.title: Intriguing at First, Exhausting Over Time
reviews.text:
Everweave is an app that gradually pulls you deeper into its experience, but not always in a satisfying way. Instead of making you feel like you’re gaining more control or understanding, it can sometimes feel like the app is simply taking more of your time and attention.

The more you use Everweave, the more it seems to draw on personal thoughts, memories, and emotions to keep the experience going. There’s something interesting about that idea, but it can also become repetitive and draining. After a while, the experience starts to feel less personal, even though it’s built around personal material.

That seems to be part of Everweave’s design rather than an accidental problem. It isn’t necessarily trying to give you a clear sense of progress or resolution. Instead, it keeps the experience going by continually working with whatever you bring to it. For some people that could be compelling, but for me it eventually felt exhausting and a little empty. There are some intriguing ideas here, but I wish the app did more with them instead of stretching them out for so long.

reviews.title: Current opinion as F2P
reviews.text:
Personally I love DnD to its full capacity and had fun playing the app for some time being. However, my current rating is not a 5/5 due to two things
- First being that some of my responses that I have given produce the exact same response that was given previously, using an already limited resource that is messages that refreshes MONTHLY. I was not too excited to see I had to repeat what I do and say as I feel if I don't maximize my own response (i.e. giving a statement, action and then another statement purely to build the scene) then it makes the requirement to respond with a single action or a single phrase feel somewhat dry.
- Secondly, although it is a LLM and it does suggest to be very descriptive to be immersive, sometimes it disregards what was written moments before or something that has been pre-established as a hard line. In my case there have been two instances, one where the NPC not only does not recall the events of last night, but also inherently knows information about myself that I have explicitly not shared (in character) to anyone. That personally takes it out of me a little, and although it does create some unique encounters, this somewhat defeats the purpose of me writing about my background.

Overall, I see potential with the app, and the instances where I got to roll dice for role-play or for combat was exciting. However, I think I will continue sticking with rolling (the dice) with my peers. Other wise, I might check out the app again in a few weeks once my message limit is refreshed.

reviews.title: Amazing
reviews.text:
This has been a great and fun example on why AI is not the way to play D&D, or any “skill” based RPG experienced. Wow, such an amazing diversity of races. A whopping… 8. Wow. And all the classes? 6 classes. All with their character archetypes baked into them. So much character flexibility. And we got all these places to visit. All of them are so unique! Ooh an upside down forest. No normal walk through normal woods? Who wants that? Nothing interesting happens in normal woods. 

Ooh but now we get to the RP. We get to roll dice for everything. Isn’t that cool? You just wanna go for a walk? Cool, make a stealth check. Either you make a loud noise and you “STOP IN YOUR TRACKS” and the whole area wakes up, or you are “moving with the grace of a predator.” That’s cool. No one would want to just be normal and WALK, right? Hmm, what a curious little rock on the ground. I wonder what that is? What’s that? Sleight of hand? Ohhh, yeah, I gotta be sneaky grabbing a rock without the nobody around me noticing, that makes sense. I just made an athletics check to drink water. I gulped like an absolute pro. Isn’t this really a fun story? My character feels so relatable. Thank you, Everweave, for such a compelling story.
